subject: ventures/horse-boarding-stall-profit-calculator
professional: a boarding barn manager or equine extension agent who builds horse-enterprise budgets. They would check first that the per-horse margin (board less feed, bedding and labour) and the break-even board price come out of the stated algebra, how care labour is costed (hours per horse per month at a wage), whether fixed costs include depreciation and interest on the barn investment, and whether full, partial and pasture board can be priced separately

evidence.correctness: Ran compute() through node on the shipped calc.mjs and recomputed by hand from first principles (unit economics: horses x (collected board+extras - feed - bedding - labour) - fixed), not from the author's tests. (a) SAMPLE (20 stalls, 85%, $550 board, $40 extras, $160 feed, $55 bedding, 20 min/day, $15/h, $3,000 fixed, 3% unpaid): hand 17 horses, income 590 x 0.97 = 572.30, labour 20 x 30.4/60 x 15 = 152.00, margin 205.30, profit 17 x 205.30 - 3000 = 490.10; tool profit 490.1, margin 205.3. Break-even horses 3000/205.30 = 14.613 (73.06%); tool 14.6128 / 73.064. Break-even board (3000/17 + 367)/0.97 - 40 = 520.28; tool 520.28. Target board (5000/17 + 367)/0.97 - 40 = 641.56; tool 641.56. (b) A second barn the author never used (10 stalls, 80%, $600 board, $200 feed, $60 bedding, 30 min/day at $18, $2,500 fixed, no extras or bad debt): hand 8 horses, labour 30 x 30.4/60 x 18 x 8 = 2,188.80, profit 4800 - 2080 - 2188.80 - 2500 = -1,968.80, break-even board 2500/8 + 260 + 273.60 = 846.10; tool -1968.8 and 846.1, with the 'Even full' (376.5%) finding. (c) Calendar standard: 365/12 = 30.4167 days/month, the tool hard-codes 30.4; on the sample that moves profit from 488.68 (standard) to 490.10 (tool), $1.42 or 0.3%, a rounding choice, not an error a user would act on. (d) Hourly-pay finding: (490.10 + 2584)/172.27 h = $17.85/h; tool $17.85. All recomputed outputs agree to the cent.
evidence.completeness: README/page claims checked end to end: monthly profit, per stall, break-even occupancy, break-even and target board, occupancy table 50-100% plus current, findings (loss, short of target, unreachable, >100%, within 10 points, hourly pay, unpaid board >=5%), text summary and CSV download (code read, sweepCsv run), print, usage opt-out, blank optional fields, error messages. All present and working in calc.mjs runs; the served page https://marisstella.app/horse-boarding-stall-profit-calculator/ returned 200 and its llms.txt points at marisstella.app (the source github.io link is rewritten at deploy). README test command from the repo root runs 21/21. No TODOs or stubs. 3.
evidence.verification: `cd ventures/horse-boarding-stall-profit-calculator && node --test '*.test.mjs'`: 21 tests, 21 pass, 0.14 s. Tests pin the headline profit to the stated rule, round-trip break-even and target prices, and check validation. Six mutations with quality_mutate.py in private copies: DAYS 30.4 -> 30 caught; break-even price dropping `- p.extras` caught; but the occupancy table's profit dropping the unpaid share (calc.mjs:43) SURVIVED (the sweep test checks only ordering and row count), the 10-point break-even warning threshold 10 -> 5 SURVIVED, the hourly-pay finding using profit instead of profit + labour SURVIVED (a wrong dollar figure shown to the user), and the unpaid-board finding >= 5 -> > 5 SURVIVED. 4 of 6 survived, including two user-visible numbers. 2.
evidence.craft: Read calc.mjs (100 lines), index.html script, usage.mjs, all three test files. Pure functions, clear validation messages, escaped HTML, money rounded only at output. Defects: occupancy accepts 0.85 as 0.85 percent with no hint (calc.mjs:25), so a user who types a fraction gets 0.17 horses and a large loss; DAYS = 30.4 is an approximation of 365/12; very long one-line expressions in compute() and the findings; profit is computed twice by two formulas (compute line 50 and profitAt line 43), which is how the sweep mutant can drift unseen. 3.
evidence.claims: Checked: 'Nothing uploaded' (no fetch/XHR/beacon in index.html, calc.mjs or usage.mjs, read); 'a test in the code asserts there are no network calls' (page.test.mjs:20-21 covers index.html and calc.mjs but not usage.mjs, which also has none: backed with a gap); usage counting local-only and off under DNT/GPC (usage.mjs read); the formula in 'What it does' matches calc.mjs exactly; 'It does not know what other barns charge' and VENTURE.yaml 'no market rate is claimed' hold (SAMPLE labelled illustrative); disclaimer present (No warranty, not legal/tax/accounting/financial advice, verify before changing a rate) and asserted by page.test.mjs; 'Not decided' lists zoning, insurance, contracts, tax, depreciation, board-type mix. 3.
evidence.fitness: Walked the job of a 20-stall owner deciding whether to raise board: enter costs, read break-even board and the occupancy table, download CSV. It answers that for a single-price barn. A barn manager hits in the first hour: no full/partial/pasture board mix (most small barns mix them; listed as not decided), labour only as per-horse minutes, so fixed chores (arena, fencing, maintenance) must be folded into fixed costs by hand, no depreciation or return on the barn/land investment, no seasonal hay price or feed calculator from bale weight and price. Usable as a first-pass worksheet, not as the enterprise budget an extension agent would build. 2.
evidence.domain: Compared with the structure of extension horse-boarding enterprise budgets (University of Maryland RES-10 and Ohio State as summarised by a web search; the PDF fetch failed through the proxy, so their figures are not confirmed here): those split variable costs per horse (hay, grain, bedding, farrier/vet if included, labour in hours per horse per month) from fixed costs including depreciation, interest on investment, insurance and taxes. The tool's margin/break-even algebra is the standard contribution-margin method and is right; it departs in leaving depreciation and capital return out of the model (users can type them into fixed costs, but are not prompted), and its example 20 min/day (about 10 h/month per horse) sits well below the roughly 21-39 h/month per horse the search attributed to the Ohio State and Maryland budgets (unconfirmed), so the worked example likely flatters profit. 2.

mutations.change: const unpaid = profit + labour; -> const unpaid = profit;

defects.what: The occupancy table's profit (profitAt) is a second formula separate from the headline profit, and no test pins its values: dropping the unpaid-board share from it leaves every test green, so the table could disagree with the headline unseen
Hourly-pay finding and the warning thresholds (10-point margin, 5% unpaid board) are untested: computing the hourly figure from profit alone (a wrong dollar figure shown to the owner) survives

One board price and per-horse labour only: no full/partial/pasture mix, no fixed (non-per-horse) labour, no depreciation or interest on the barn investment, which extension horse-boarding budgets carry; users are not prompted to add them to fixed costs
Occupancy typed as a fraction (0.85) is accepted as 0.85 percent with no warning
Days per month hard-coded as 30.4 rather than 365/12 (30.4167); 0.3% of profit on the sample

Worked example uses 20 care minutes per horse per day (about 10 h/month), well below the labour hours per horse that extension budgets reportedly use (about 21-39 h/month, unconfirmed here), so the example likely flatters profit; labelled illustrative
FAQ says a test asserts there are no network calls, but the test scans index.html and calc.mjs only, not usage.mjs (which has none today)

verdict: A small, correct contribution-margin worksheet: every output recomputed by hand on two barns (profit 490.10 and -1,968.80, break-even board 520.28 and 846.10, target board 641.56, hourly pay $17.85) matches to the cent, the disclaimer and limits are honest, and the served page works. It misses the bar on verification: 4 of 6 seeded mutants survived, including the occupancy table's profit formula and the hourly-pay figure, both user-visible. A barn manager or extension agent would also want board-type mix, fixed labour and depreciation/capital return before using it as an enterprise budget.
